problem: Most VLM-based robot work predicts low-level actions directly from multimodal input, which needs large amounts of expert demonstration data (e.g. generated by trained RL policies). Hierarchical VLM+RL, where the VLM gives high-level guidance and an RL policy handles locomotion, is little explored for quadrupeds.
motivation: RL (PPO) already gives stable quadruped locomotion, while VLMs can interpret language instructions and visual context. Splitting high-level navigation from low-level control could avoid the demonstration-data dependence of end-to-end VLM action prediction.
key_idea: A VLM navigator reads the text instruction, egocentric vision and proprioceptive state and outputs heading adjustments and forward/stop commands, which a PPO-trained RL locomotion controller executes on a quadruped.
insight: Only the abstract was available, so no ablations are visible. The abstract reports that a hierarchical VLM+RL split works well in unobstructed settings (failure below 10%), but in complex environments success falls to 66%. The stated weak points are obstacle-avoidance reasoning and stop prediction.
method: VLM navigator: takes text instruction, egocentric image and proprioceptive state, and outputs a heading adjustment plus a forward/stop command
RL locomotion controller: a PPO-trained quadruped policy that tracks the VLM's heading and forward commands
Hierarchical interface: high-level discrete heading/forward/stop commands connect the VLM to the low-level controller, with no demonstration data needed for the VLM

setting.backbone: VLM (unspecified in abstract) as navigator + PPO RL locomotion policy
setting.training_data: RL locomotion policy trained with PPO; VLM training details not given in abstract
setting.observation: egocentric RGB + proprioceptive state + text instruction
setting.action_space: heading adjustments and forward/stop commands passed to an RL locomotion controller
setting.privileged: none stated (navigates to a predefined target)

results: The hierarchical VLM+RL approach shows failure rates below 10% in unobstructed environments. In more complex environments, navigation success drops to 66%. No baselines are named in the abstract.
limitations: Weak obstacle-avoidance reasoning in complex environments (66% success)
Evaluated on navigation to a predefined target only
